I read the whole referee (wala-fr/CodingamePoker @ac30d97) and ported it to Python as a simulator: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-crossfish/f037db7b-a196-59d6-b8c8-4b93b15f1833/scratchpad/poker_research/poker_sim.py. I tested the port against real games. I downloaded 120 recent replays involving the current top-10 agents (27 two-player, 45 three-player, 48 four-player) through the public API. Each replay was driven by its referee seed and the recorded bot outputs. The simulator reproduced all 120/120 exactly: who acts at every step, the hand count, the round counter and the final scores (validate_replays.py). The spec below is therefore checked against the live server, not just read from the code.

The biggest surprise is not in the statement. Every player who is not the big blind posts the small blind every hand (Board.java:204-218). The statement only says "blinds 5/10". The effect is that the preflop pot is 1.5 BB heads-up, 2 BB with 3 players and 2.5 BB with 4. The replays confirm it: the first pot is $20 in 3-player games and $25 in 4-player games. The test 7_check/test1.txt also shows the UTG folding and losing 10 at 10/20. Non-BB players only need 0.5 BB more to call.

Blinds are 10*2^floor(h/10) for the BB, with the SB at half. Hands 1-9 play 5/10, hands 10-19 play 10/20, and so on. The level rises when handNb%10==0 (Board.java:220-230).

The big blind moves to the next seat that still has chips (Board.java:183-192). The small blind is the previous live seat and the dealer is the live seat before that. Heads-up, the dealer is the small blind (Board.java:146-180). There is no dead button or dead small blind. Preflop, the first player after the BB acts first. On later streets, the first live player after the dealer acts first, so heads-up the BB acts first after the flop (Board.java:232-253, 329).

A player who cannot cover a blind posts everything they have. Any player not in the SB seat with fewer chips than the BB is all-in automatically (Board.java:209-214). Preflop, a call is always at least one BB total, even if the BB is all-in for less (Board.java:468-479).

"BET x" means x chips added now, not "raise to x". The offered BET_x is the minimum raise, where x = minRaise + lastTotalRoundBet - myRoundBet (ActionUtils.java:352-353). The minimum raise is the BB for the first bet, otherwise the size of the last full raise (Board.java:255-275).

A short all-in does not change the bet level or the minimum raise. Only the last full raiser is limited to call or fold (ActionUtils.java:443-448, 462-464). Two consequences are non-standard. The next player can raise by as little as the last full raise over the old level, which can be less than a full raise over the all-in. Players other than the last raiser may re-raise even if they have already acted. There is a cap of 10 raises per street (Parameter.java:24, Board.java:621).

Actions are replaced rather than rejected:
- A bet at or below the call amount becomes CALL, or ALL-IN if you can't cover it.
- An undersized raise is raised to the minimum, or becomes ALL-IN if short.
- A bet at or above your stack becomes ALL-IN.
- CALL when checking is possible becomes CHECK.
- CHECK when facing a bet becomes FOLD.
- Invalid text, or "BET 0" or less, becomes FOLD.
- FOLD is never replaced (ActionUtils.java:411-505; Action.java:43-64; ActionInfo.java:78-79).

Pots and hand ranks follow standard rules. Side pots are resolved in layers and uncalled chips are returned. Odd chips go to the first winner left of the dealer (WinningCalculator.java:33-104). Hand strength is the best of the 21 five-card combinations, and suits never break ties.

Once no further betting is possible (everyone left is all-in or matched), the rest of the board is dealt with no inputs (Board.java:317-322; Referee.java:106-120). A hand with no decisions at all still uses one round, shown as "-1 NONE".

A "round" is one player decision, counted globally across all players (Referee.java:155). The cap is exactly 600 decisions. This matches the SDK's 30 s total-time quota: 600 x 50 ms = 30,000 ms (GameManager.java:38, 639-642). The winnings check comes before the cap check (Referee.java:122-131), so the 600th decision can still finish a hand. If the hand is unfinished, it is cancelled and every chip put in, including blinds, is returned (Board.java:604-611).

Scoring works like this:
- The eventual winner and any survivors score their stack.
- Eliminated players score rank - N, so a later bust scores better.
- Players who bust in the same hand are ordered by the chips they put in, which for an all-in is their stack at the start of the hand. Exact ties share a rank (Board.java:554-580, 613-619).
- A timeout folds the player and deletes their remaining stack from the game (Board.java:582-587).

Input arrives only when it is your turn (InputSender.java:49-115):
- Init lines (sent on your first turn only): SB, BB, 10, 2, buy-in, firstBBId, N, id.
- Each turn: round and handNb.
- N lines of "stack chipInPot", where chipInPot is your total for the whole hand.
- The board padded with X, then your two hole cards.
- Every action since your last turn, including your own, showing the action after replacement. ALL-IN has no amount.
- One showdown line for every hand finished since your last turn. It shows all hole cards of every player dealt in, including folded ones, even when the hand ended without a showdown. Undealt board cards stay X and players already eliminated show E_E (ShowDownInfo.java:46-50, RefereeParameter.java:12).
- The possible actions.

Time limits are 50 ms per decision and 1000 ms for each player's first decision (RefereeParameter.java:5-6; SDK GameManager.java:202).

The deck cannot be predicted. The SDK random generator is SecureRandom SHA1PRNG seeded with the game seed (MultiplayerGameManager.java:57-62). Each hand reshuffles a fresh deck and cuts it (Deck.java:23-25, 60-65), so the deck sequence does not depend on what players do. My byte-exact Python SHA1PRNG matches Java. The seeds in replays are exact, so any public replay can be rebuilt with every player's hole cards (reconstruct.py gave 22,916 decisions from 120 games).

The win-probability display is for the viewer only; bots never receive it. It enumerates every remaining board exactly, using the real hole cards of everyone still in, with a Java port of SKPokerEval. Its tables are 408k characters, far more than the 100k source limit.

In practice, top-bot games last a median of 42/46/46 hands for 2/3/4 players. They use 124/191/229 rounds on average (max 339) and never reached the 600 cap in these 120 games. Passive bots do reach it. Four calling stations (the league-1 boss plays like this) hit the cap every time at about hand 38.

Most decisions are deep. Only 12-17% happen at an effective stack of 15 BB or less, and 51-64% at more than 50 BB. But 44-54% of eliminations happen at 10 BB or less, and 69-79% at 20 BB or less. From hand 40 onward about half of all hands contain a preflop all-in.

Confirmed three ways: replay start pots of $20 (3p) and $25 (4p); test 7_check/test1.txt, where UTG folds preflop and loses 10 at 10/20; and the exact reproduction of 120 games. The statement never mentions this.

Average stack in BB for 2/3/4 players alive: hands 1-9: 240/160/120; 10-19: 120/80/60; 20-29: 60/40/30; 30-39: 30/20/15; 40-49: 15/10/7.5; 50-59: 7.5/5/3.75; 60-69: 3.75/2.5/1.9; 70-79: 1.9/1.25/0.94. M (stack divided by the preflop pot) is two-thirds, one-half and two-fifths of those figures. The full hand 1-80 table is in stack_depth_table.txt.

A round is one player decision, counted globally (Referee.java:155 incrementTurn). The cap check `turn == 600` is at Game.java:148 and Referee.java:127-131. 600 x 50 ms = 30,000 ms, which equals the SDK GAME_DURATION_HARD_QUOTA (codingame-game-engine GameManager.java:38, 639-642).

Winnings are resolved before the cap check (Referee.java:122-126 vs 127), so the 600th decision can still finish a hand. An unfinished hand is cancelled and all chips put in, including blinds, are refunded (Board.java:604-611, PlayerModel.cancelCurrentHand). Final scores are then the stacks (Board.java:613-619).

A hand with no decisions at all (everyone all-in from the blinds) uses one round and appears in the history as `round hand -1 NONE board` (Referee.java:110-114; InputUtils.java:42). Referee bug: if that happens at round 600, the round becomes 601 and roundInfos[601] (array size 601, InputSender.java:21,30) crashes the referee.

Real games (120 games from top-10 agents, fetched 2026-09-30). Final hand number mean/median/range: 2p 35.9/42/3-70; 3p 44.5/46/16-64; 4p 46.4/46/24-70. Rounds mean 124/191/229, max 339. The 600 cap was reached 0/120 times.
Decisions per hand in 4-player games, by level: 7.3 (hands 1-9), 6.7, 4.9, 3.2, 2.4, 2.2, 1.6. Preflop decisions are 52%/60%/63% of all decisions for 2/3/4-player games.

Policy study (stack_depth.py policy, 200 simulated games each). Calling stations (like the league-1 boss, config/Boss.java:54): 4p hits the cap 100% of the time at hand 38 (16 decisions per hand); 3p 100% at about hand 51; HU 3%. Passive check/call bots: 3p 98%, 4p 100%.
How hands end (hand_outcomes.py). Hands 1-29: 44-52% end preflop, 14-19% reach showdown, 6-8% contain a preflop all-in. Hands 30-39: 26% contain a preflop all-in. Hands 40-49: 48%. Hands 50-59: 54%.

Effective stack of 15 BB or less at decision time: 11.8% (2p), 15.8% (3p), 17.4% (4p) of decisions. More than 50 BB: 64%/52%/51%. Eliminations: 44%/54%/53% happen with a start-of-hand stack of 10 BB or less and 70%/79%/69% at 20 BB or less; the median bust is at about 8-11 BB (elim_depth.py).

Positions: BB moves to the next seat with chips (Board.java:183-192). SB is the first live seat before the BB and the dealer is the next one back. With exactly 2 live players the dealer is the SB (Board.java:146-180). Preflop the first actor is the first live seat after the BB. On later streets it is the first live seat after the dealer, so heads-up the BB acts first (Board.java:232-253, 329).

Short blinds: a player not in the SB seat with fewer chips than the BB posts their whole stack and is all-in (Board.java:209-214). Preflop the call amount is max(BB, max total bet) minus your total bet, so everyone must reach one BB even if the BB is all-in for less (Board.java:468-479).

BET x adds x chips; it is not 'raise to x'. The offered BET_x is the minimum raise: x = minRaise + lastTotalRoundBet - myRoundBet, where minRaise is the BB for the first bet and otherwise the last full raise (ActionUtils.java:352-356). A raise counts as full only if the increase is at least the BB (first bet) or the last full raise (Board.java:262-272).

Short all-ins do not move lastTotalRoundBet or the minimum raise. Only the last full raiser is restricted to call or fold (ActionUtils.java:443-448, 462-464), so other players may re-raise after a short all-in. Raise cap: raiseNb > 10 (Parameter.java:24, Board.java:621-623). The count starts at 1 preflop (Board.java:178) and 0 on later streets (Board.java:121).

Action replacement (ActionUtils.java:411-505). CALL becomes CHECK when checking is possible, or ALL-IN when short. BET at or below the call amount becomes CALL or ALL-IN. BET by the last full raiser, or at the raise cap, becomes CALL. BET at or above your stack becomes ALL-IN. An undersized raise becomes the minimum BET (or ALL-IN). CHECK when facing a bet becomes FOLD. ALL-IN by the last raiser becomes CALL. FOLD is never replaced.

Output parsing: split on ';' and keep the first part, then uppercase and trim (Referee.java:161-168). `BET_x` is accepted and `ALL_IN` works as well as `ALL-IN` (Action.java:43-64, ActionType.java:6-11). Anything unparseable becomes FOLD (ActionInfo.java:78-79), including `RAISE 200`, `CALL 10`, `BET  200` with a double space, or a non-integer amount.

Side pots are resolved in layers: take the smallest live contribution, split it among the best hands, and repeat. Whatever is left over goes back to the player who put it in. The odd chip goes to the first winner clockwise from dealer+1 (WinningCalculator.java:33-104). Best hand is chosen from 21 five-card combinations (Hand.calculateBestFiveCardhand) with standard rankings, and the wheel ranks below a 6-high straight (FiveCardHand.java:42-77).

Showdown info: every hole card of every player dealt into the hand is revealed, including folded hands and hands that ended without a showdown, because SHOW_FOLDED_CARDS=true (ShowDownInfo.java:46-50; RefereeParameter.java:12). Players already eliminated show `E_E`. Undealt board cards stay `X`. Burn cards are never shown.

Stdin order (InputSender.java:49-115). Init lines on your first turn only: 5, 10, 10, 2, buyIn (4800/N), firstBigBlindId, N, id. Each turn: round; handNb; N lines of `stack chipInPot` (chipInPot is your whole-hand total); board (X-padded); your cards; actionNb plus lines of `round hand pid ACTION board` covering everything since your last turn, your own last action first, post-replacement, with ALL-IN carrying no amount; showDownNb plus lines of `hand board c0_c1_..`; possibleActionNb plus the actions.

Scoring and ranking. Eliminated players score rank - N, where rank 0 is the first out (Board.java:554-580). Players busting in the same hand are ordered by chips put in that hand (for an all-in, the start-of-hand stack); ties share the score. Survivors and the winner score their stack (Board.java:613-619; Referee.onEnd 284-298). A timeout folds the player and deletes their remaining stack from the game (Board.java:582-587; Referee.java:170-179).

RNG: the referee uses gameManager.getRandom() (Referee.java:60), and the SDK makes that SecureRandom SHA1PRNG seeded with the game seed (MultiplayerGameManager.java:57-62), not java.util.Random. The first BB is nextInt(N) (Referee.java:64). Every hand shuffles a fresh 2C,2D,..,AS deck with Collections.shuffle, then cuts it with nextInt(52) (Deck.java:17-25, 60-65). My Python SHA1PRNG port matches Java byte for byte, including Java's signed-byte carry.

The seed in replays (refereeInput `seed=...`) is exact. With the simulator, any public replay can be turned into a complete hand history with everyone's hole cards: reconstruct.py wrote 22,916 decisions from 120 games to decisions.jsonl.

Timing: 50 ms per decision; each player's first decision gets 1000 ms (RefereeParameter.java:5-6; SDK GameManager.java:202 `hasNeverBeenExecuted() ? firstTurnMaxTime : turnMaxTime`). MAX_REFEREE_TURN is 10000 frames (not binding).

The win-probability display is exact full enumeration of the remaining board, using all live players' real hole cards and a Java port of SKPokerEval (WinPercentUtils.java:100-205). It is shown only in the viewer (PlayerUI.java:137-147) and never sent to bots. Its lookup tables total about 408k characters, which is more than the 100k source limit.

Leaderboard: 192 players; the top league has 42 (lowest in it scores 7.11); top TrueSkill 30.65 (Waffle3z, C++). Languages in the top league: Python3 20, C++ 7, Java 3, C 3, other 9. Waffle3z's last 134 battles were 57 four-player, 51 three-player and 26 two-player.
design_implications: Solve with the real blind structure. Because every non-BB player posts the SB, preflop pots are 2 BB (3p) or 2.5 BB (4p), and completing costs only 0.5 BB (6:1 in 4p). Standard 6-max, heads-up or push/fold charts are miscalibrated here. Precompute push/fold and open/defend strategies for exactly this structure (N=2,3,4 live, stacks 0-25 BB) and embed them compactly.

Two regimes. About half of all decisions happen deep (more than 50 BB, hands 1-25), but about 70-80% of eliminations happen at 20 BB or less, and from hand 40 onward about half of hands contain a preflop all-in. The short-stack preflop game (push, fold, call-off) is small and nearly solvable, and it decides most outcomes. Deep postflop play is where a learned policy plus search could add value on top.

The payoff is rank-based, not chips. In 3-4 player games, finishing 2nd vs 3rd matters, so terminal utilities for self-play or search should use ICM or rank (e.g., Malmuth-Harville with rank payoffs, or a TrueSkill proxy). Heads-up, chip EV is roughly correct. The 600-round cap never binds between competent bots (0/120), but against passive lower-league bots it can: the unfinished last hand is refunded and ranking is by stack, so track `round`.

Opponent modelling gets exact labels. Every hand reveals all players' hole cards, including folded ones, so after each hand you know exactly which cards produced each opponent action. Per-opponent frequencies conditioned on hand strength (open, 3-bet, fold-to-shove and bluff frequencies) can be fit within a game, from about 40-110 decisions per opponent. There is no memory across games, so the prior must come from the population.

Population data from public replays. Exact seeds plus the byte-exact SHA1PRNG mean public replays reconstruct into complete-information trajectories of the top bots (22.9k decisions from 120 games in minutes). Uses: behaviour-cloning sparring partners, training belief or value nets on realistic play, and measuring how exploitable current top bots are. Scale up gently with respect to the API and the terms of service.

Engine fidelity matters for search and RL. Replicate the non-standard rules exactly: every player posts the SB; short-blind posters are forced all-in; the preflop call is at least one BB; the minimum raise is measured from the last full raise level; after a short all-in, only the last full raiser is locked to call; raise cap of 10; side pots and odd chips; NONE rounds; the 600 cap with refund. poker_sim.py plus validate_replays.py is a regression oracle for a C++ port.

Beliefs are cheap in poker. There are at most 1,326 hole-card combinations per opponent, and all cards are revealed afterwards, so exact Bayesian range tracking (a 1,326-entry vector per opponent, updated by the modelled policy's action likelihoods) replaces Ataraxos's learned belief network. Sampling hands, running short rollouts and taking a regularised MMD step toward the policy fits in 50 ms in C++ with a small bet abstraction.

Action space. Every output is made legal by replacement, so fold / CALL / min-raise / 0.5, 1 and 2x pot / ALL-IN is enough. `CALL` is a universally safe output: it becomes CHECK or ALL-IN as needed. Never output CHECK when facing a bet, because it becomes FOLD. Reconstruct street-level bets and the minimum raise from the history or the BET_x hint, since chipInPot is the whole-hand total and ALL-IN lines carry no amount.

Code-size and time budget. The SKPokerEval tables (about 408k characters) don't fit in 100k. Generate a fast 7-card evaluator's tables during the 1000 ms first decision, or use a compact bit-based evaluator, and keep network weights within the crossfish-style compressed budget. Each player makes at most about 110 decisions per game at 50 ms each.

Testing. The deck sequence depends only on the seed, not on actions, so local evaluation can use duplicate poker (same seeds, rotated seats) to cut variance a lot. The live RNG is SHA1PRNG and cannot be predicted, so deck prediction is not a possible exploit.

Handle all table sizes. The top player's games were about 43% four-player, 38% three-player and 19% heads-up, and 3-4 player games shrink to heads-up during play. The policy must cover N = 2, 3 and 4 live players with arbitrary seat and blind positions, derived from firstBigBlindId plus BB rotation to the next seat with chips.
open_questions: Does CodinGame suspend bot processes between turns, so no thinking on opponents' time? The referee and SDK don't settle this; it would need an experiment.
How does CodinGame's TrueSkill weight 2nd vs 3rd vs 4th and handle tied scores in 3-4 player games? This determines the right ICM or rank utility.
How does matchmaking choose the player count (2/3/4)? The mix quoted comes from one player's last 134 battles only.
Rate limits and terms of service for scraping thousands of replays for training data (findLastBattlesByAgentId returns about 134 games per agent per call).
The current SDK master adds SOFT_TIMELIMIT_EXTRA=50 ms of slack; the referee's pom pins SDK 4.4.2. The real timeout margin was not measured.
The round-601 crash (NONE round exactly at the cap) has never been seen in practice. What the platform does with a crashed referee is unknown.

research.summary:
Summary: the CodinGame Poker arena is small, noisy, and full of hand-written heuristic bots. Nobody in it runs a real solver. The #1 bot is only slightly better than the rest of the top league. This comes from a leaderboard dump, 2,495 recent battles of the top 37 players, and 371 replays. I rebuilt all 371 replays exactly (every player's hole cards and every action) by re-running the open-source referee with each game's seed.

Field size and structure: 192 bots in 2 leagues (150 in the lower league plus its boss, 42 in the top league). Python has 90 bots overall and 3 of the top 6 (BrandV #3, Tuo #5, JuMaKre #6), so CPU time is not what separates bots today. The top league includes 8 CodinGame-made LLM bots. [CG]Gemini-Python sits at #26 (score 25.42) and [CG]OpenAIGPT4o at #35, so getting into the top league takes little. The arena is active: 19 new submissions in September 2026, and the top 3 all resubmitted between 25 and 30 Sept.

Written material: the official forum thread has no replies (728 views). I found no post-mortems. The only public bot code on GitHub is gpoussel/copro poker.ts. It is a Monte-Carlo equity-versus-random-hands plus pot-odds bot, and it ranks #45, at the top of the lower league. The other public repo is the referee, wala-fr/CodingamePoker. Most discussion probably happens on Discord.

What the top bots are, from their public debug messages and my replay statistics:
- Waffle3z (#1, C++) is a loose-aggressive steal machine. It plays 70% of hands and raises 64% preflop. It raises 90% of pots nobody has opened yet, mostly 2-6 big blinds (BB). After the flop it bets 97% of the time when checked to, sized at 0.5 or 0.1 of the pot. It folds 62% when facing a bet and calls only 33% of all-ins.
- kovi (#2) runs explicit rules. Its messages include "rule", "rnd", "push #bb #way", "shortfold-vs-raise" and "anti-maniac". It is tight: plays 26% of hands, folds 79% when raised, and bets pot-sized.
- BrandV (#3) is loose. It shoves all-in 66% of the time at 10-20BB and calls raises 68%.
- Zylo (#4) is tight-aggressive.
- Tuo (#5) and AGSigma (#10) are pure push/fold bots. Tuo shoves or folds even 120-240BB deep, and still finishes ahead of Waffle3z 56% of the time head to head.
- JuMaKre (#6), supernakash, kozlov-ma and Tux4711 compare Monte-Carlo equity with pot odds. Their messages look like "pf call e= need=", "shove ev=" and "eq: 0.479,0.0452s".
- MaxFerrer (#9) mixes a "GTO.PF.RSHV" push/fold chart with "XPT.*" exploit rules.
- There are also calling stations (kozlov-ma limps 87%, trictrac 80%) and maniacs (SmogyY and UnTypedScript raise to 25-100BB and call 100% of all-ins).

What decides games: blinds double every 10 hands and there are only 4,800 chips in total. Games last a median of 40-47 hands, and none of 371 reached the 600-round cap. 56% of bust-outs happen at under 10BB and 72% at under 20BB. 51% of chips change hands at under 20BB effective. 80% of hands end without a showdown, and 15% have a preflop all-in. Tables are 41% 4-player, 34% 3-player and 25% heads-up.

How the ranking works: final order is by elimination order, then stack. The score is placement-only TrueSkill (mean minus 3 deviations): 10 placement games, then about 100 more played one after another. Chip margin does not count, so survival (ICM-like thinking) matters at 3-4 players.

How close the field is: against top-league opponents, #1 finishes ahead of a given opponent only 61.1% ±4.7% of the time. #2-#6 are at 54-58% (±6-7%). Matchups are not transitive.

Common weaknesses:
- Folding too much to small opens: kovi 78%, insomnia_rooster 77%, Zylo 68%, wala 67%.
- Folding too much to small bets after the flop: insomnia_rooster 86%, MaxFerrer 83%, Tux4711 71%.
- Calling stations that should be value-bet and never bluffed.
- Maniacs whose calling range is roughly the top 60% of hands.
- Push/fold bots whose blinds can be stolen.

Every hand ends with all hole cards shown, folded ones included, so a bot sees the exact hands behind every opponent action. That makes it realistic to adapt to an opponent within one 40-70-hand game.

Ranking rules: TrueSkill on finishing placement. A new submission plays 10 parallel placement games against opponents from the whole leaderboard, then about 100 sequential games. Its initial position is based on mean minus 3 deviations. To be promoted you must finish ahead of the boss (https://forum.codingame.com/t/how-is-the-rank-for-single-finished-bot-programming-computed/194147). JuMaKre, submitted the same day, already had 84 battles.

Timeouts eliminate the bot and do happen in the top league: deuwii timed out on its first action in game 906358479, and [CG]CohereCommandA-Python timed out once. Turn limit is 50 ms (1000 ms on the first turn).
design_implications: The field is beatable but noisy. Nobody runs a solver or learned policy. The top bots are rules, charts, and equity-versus-pot-odds, and a pure push/fold bot is #5. Even so, #1 finishes ahead of a given top-league opponent only about 61% of the time. A stronger bot should reach #1, but proving it needs hundreds of games, and one ~100-game submission leaves a ±5% band.

Most of the result is decided at short stacks. 72% of bust-outs happen under 20BB and games last about 40-47 hands because blinds double every 10 hands. Push/fold and reshove play at 5-25BB, for 2-4 players, is the highest-value thing to get right. It is small enough to solve almost exactly offline, and in a 100k-character source limit a table beats a network.

Optimise finishing position, not chips. TrueSkill uses placement only: elimination order, then stack, and chip margin is ignored. At 3-4 players (75% of games), survival and ICM-style risk aversion change the right calling ranges. Any self-play or MMD training should use placement as the reward, not chip EV.

Deep-stack play (hands 1-~25, 120-240BB) is lower-stakes because blinds are tiny. A simple tight-aggressive or LAG baseline with good postflop fold discipline is probably enough there. Waffle3z makes most of its edge at 20-80BB (+0.56 to +0.94 BB/hand), which suggests stealing and aggression pay off in the middle phase.

The field's weaknesses have direct counters. Steal wide and make small raises against the many bots that fold 64-78% to small opens (kovi, Zylo, insomnia_rooster, MaxFerrer). Bet small and often after the flop against those folding 70-86% to half-pot bets. Value-bet thin and never bluff the limpers and calling stations. Call off wider against the maniacs. Waffle3z's 97% bet-when-checked-to and 62% fold-to-bet pattern invites check-raises.

All cards are revealed after every hand, folded ones included, so within one 40-70-hand game a bot learns exactly which hands each opponent plays each way. Classifying opponents online (nit, push/fold, station, maniac, LAG) and shifting away from equilibrium, as kovi does with its 'anti-maniac' rule, is cheap and likely worth a lot. An Ataraxos/MMD self-play policy is deliberately non-exploitative. It is best used as a robust baseline that holds up in this non-transitive field (Tuo beats Waffle3z, which beats Tux4711), with a separate exploit layer on top.

Public replays and the open-source referee make a strong dataset possible. The replayer I built reconstructs every hole card and action from any arena game. Hundreds of top-bot games can be harvested for imitation or opponent-model pretraining, to build a local sparring pool of style clones (LAG, nit, push/fold, station, maniac), and to test locally with the exact arena RNG and rules (SHA1PRNG seed, RAISE_CAP=10, BET amount = chips added).

Compute budget: 50 ms per turn is plenty. Python Monte-Carlo equity bots finish #3, #5 and #6, and supernakash spends about 45 ms per decision. A C++ bot can afford small-net inference plus MC rollouts or a single tabular MMD-style search step. The binding constraints are the 100k-character source limit and getting the strategy right. Timeouts mean elimination, so keep hard time guards (bots have timed out in the top league).

The top league is easy to reach: [CG]Gemini-Python is #26, and the lower-league boss limps 43% of unopened pots and folds 95% when raised. Budget effort for the top-10 fight, where edges are about 2-6 percentage points of pairwise placement. Expect the target to move, since the top 3 resubmitted in the last week.

research.summary:
Short answer: yes. The Ataraxos techniques can be used for CodinGame Poker, but poker only needs about half of them. Ataraxos needed an autoregressive belief transformer and 40-ply rollouts because Stratego has about 10^33 hidden configurations. In NLHE each opponent's hidden state is at most 1,326 combos, which the Ataraxos paper itself notes (paper.txt:28). So the belief becomes an exact Bayes update over combos, and rollouts only have to reach the end of the hand (at most 4 streets). Two pieces transfer directly. (1) MMD-damped self-play RL (PPO + reverse-KL to a magnet + annealing) to train a small policy/value net on the actual tournament: 2-4 seats, doubling blinds, rank payoff. (2) The one-step update-equivalence search pi' ∝ exp[(log pi_theta + eta*q_hat + eta*alpha*log rho)/(1+eta*alpha)]. In poker this search is cheap. More importantly, it becomes a tunable exploitation operator: plug an opponent model into the belief likelihood and the rollouts, and the KL-to-pi_theta term bounds how far the move can drift from the blueprint.

Setting (from the referee source and 371 replayed top-bot games):
- 50 ms per turn, 1000 ms for the first turn (RefereeParameter.java:5-6).
- Folded hands are revealed too (RefereeParameter.java:13, ShowDownInfo.java:50).
- Eliminated players are scored by bust order; players who bust in the same hand are ranked by the chips they started it with (Board.java:555-578).
- The 600-turn cap never fired in the replays. Every game ended with one survivor, after a median of 40 hands (HU start) or 46-47 hands (3-4p start).
- Finishing order feeds TrueSkill. With equal ratings, TrueSkill mean updates imply payouts (1,0), (1,.5,0) and (1,.645,.355,0) for 2, 3 and 4 players.
- Heads-up, P(win) is linear in chips, so chip-EV is essentially correct.
- 3-4 handed, ICM with these payouts creates large risk premia. Calling off an all-in needs 60% equity with 3 equal stacks, 64.6% with 4, and 73.7% for a big stack against the other big stack when two short stacks remain.
- About half of eliminations happen at ≤10 BB and 69-79% at ≤20 BB. Still, most 3-4-alive hands are played at >30 BB effective, so deep play matters too.

(a) Push/fold:
- Miltersen–Sørensen (AAMAS'07): heads-up at ≤6.7 BB effective, restricting yourself to jam/fold costs at most 1.4% of win probability.
- Ganzfried–Sandholm (AAMAS'08, IJCAI'09) solved 3-player jam/fold tournaments at 7.5 BB. They used ICM-initialized value iteration plus fictitious play (no player gains >0.1% of max payoff by deviating). They found ICM is off by up to $2.99 per $100 pool, and that tournament strategies differ sharply from chip-EV ones.
- I also solved HU jam/fold Nash myself (in chips, with card removal). SB jam / BB call: 71/62% at 5 BB, 58/38% at 10 BB, 46/28% at 15 BB, 40/22% at 20 BB.
- The value jam/fold guarantees the SB is positive only up to about 7 BB. It is −0.045, −0.127 and −0.183 BB/hand at 10, 15 and 20 BB. So pure push/fold is near-optimal only up to roughly 8-10 BB heads-up.
- FGS (future game simulation) fixes ICM's blindness to blinds and position; a learned place-distribution value head does the same job.

(b) HU deep-stack methods:
- DeepStack, Libratus, ReBeL, Student of Games and Pluribus all need 10^4 to 10^6 core-hours or GPU/TPU clusters, and seconds per decision.
- Tabular blueprints are far too big for 100k characters (Slumbot needed 2 TB of RAM to compute, Baby Tartanian8 18 TB).
- Modicum is the cheapest principled one (700 core-hours, 4-core laptop), but it takes about 20 s per hand, roughly 400x over the 50 ms budget.
- AlphaHoldem (3 days on 8 GPUs, PPO-style self-play, 2.9 ms per decision) shows end-to-end RL works in HUNL. That is the Ataraxos route, and it is the realistic one here, with a much smaller network.

(c) Multiplayer:
- Pluribus states outright that its methods have no guarantees outside 2-player zero-sum.
- Szafron et al. (3-player Kuhn) show equilibria where one player can shift utility between the other two.
- So 3-4 handed, equilibrium play is not "safe". Rank is won through exploitation and ICM survival logic.

(d) MMD on poker benchmarks:
- MMD converges exponentially fast to QRE on Kuhn and Leduc.
- With annealing it is competitive with CFR; CFR+ is still best.
- It reaches 0.08 exploitability in Leduc in under 1,000 iterations; F-FoReL needed about 200k.
- MMD-based decision-time search (the update-equivalence paper) was validated only on tabular Kuhn/Leduc analogues (AQRE and annealed-Nash convergence), not on Hold'em.
- Across 7,000 runs, NFSP/PSRO/ESCHER/R-NaD did not outperform generic policy-gradient methods (MMD/PPO/PPG) (Rudolph et al.).

(e) Opponent modelling:
- Relevant methods: RNR, DBR, Ganzfried–Sandholm safe exploitation ("risk only what you have won"), Bayes' Bluff, Dirichlet-prior Bayesian exploitation, and implicit portfolio modelling.
- CodinGame's full reveal of folded cards is a major advantage. The per-decision likelihood is exact and unbiased, so the showdown-censoring bias (Guo 2026) does not arise.
- But data is scarce. Each opponent makes a median of 55-63 decisions per game, only 14-23 of them postflop, and opponent identities are not in the input. Strong priors are therefore essential: a population model, or a library of cloned leaderboard bots with a Bayesian posterior over which one you face.
- Exploitation gains are large compared with equilibrium edges. At 10 BB HU push/fold, best-responding to a nit caller gains +0.278 BB/hand over Nash. A one-step MMD update with eta=3 or 10 captures 15% or 91% of that gain, while the worst-case value falls from −0.045 to −0.067 or −0.328. So eta is the safety dial.

Ataraxos components, sorted:
- Directly useful: MMD-PPO self-play with annealing; the value head (as a learned FGS/ICM); one-step MMD search with the KL-to-policy term; the power-law schedules.
- Unnecessary: the belief transformer (replaced by exact Bayes over 1,326 combos), the setup network, depth-40 rollouts, and multi-million-parameter nets (they cannot fit in 100k characters anyway).
- Needs modification:
  - Terminal values: tournament equity with the TrueSkill payouts, or a place-distribution value head.
  - Chance nodes: common random numbers across actions, and exact equity once all-in.
  - Advantage filtering: only on low-variance advantages (privileged critic, all-in EV); otherwise it selects card luck.
  - Exploitation: an opponent model in the belief and rollouts, with DBR-style confidence mixing and an eta budget.
  - Multi-way: joint belief by rejection sampling on card removal, and no 2p0s guarantee.
  - Continuous opponent bet sizes: feed them to the net as inputs, so no action translation is needed.

ICM (Malmuth-Harville; Harville 1973 JASA, Malmuth 1987; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Chip_Model) with those payouts (SP/pf/icm2.py): required win probability to call off an equal-stack all-in (no dead money): HU 50.0%, 3p equal stacks 60.0%, 4p equal 64.6%, 4p (600,1800,1800,600) big vs big 73.7%, short vs short 55.7%, chip leader 2400 calling 400 short 51.9%, 3 left of 4 (1600x3, payouts 1/.645/.355) 59.2%.

Miltersen & Sorensen, AAMAS 2007 (as restated in Ganzfried-Sandholm AAMAS'08, SP/lit/gs08.txt ~l.150-160): HU tournament 8000 chips, blinds 300/600 (effective stack <= 6.7BB): V1(G1,s1)+V2(G2,8000-s1) >= 0.986, i.e. restricting yourself to jam/fold loses at most 1.4% win probability; optimal strategy randomizes with at most one hand per state; no fixed hand ranking; single-hand and tournament strategies almost identical HU.

Ganzfried & Sandholm, AAMAS 2008 (https://aamas.csc.liv.ac.uk/Proceedings/aamas08/proceedings/pdf/paper/AAMAS08_0313.pdf): 3-player jam/fold, 13,500 chips, 300/600 blinds (4500 each = 7.5BB), 946 stack states, fictitious play inside value iteration initialised with ICM; no player can gain > $0.0488 (<0.1% of max payoff); ICM deviation from computed values avg $0.37, max $2.99 per $100 pool (big blind forced to post 2/3 of stack); tournament vs single-hand frequencies differ widely, e.g. BB jam after jam/jam 0.021 vs 0.197, SB jam after jam 0.088 vs 0.234. IJCAI 2009 follow-up (https://www.ijcai.org/Abstract/09/034): provably-equilibrium variants, epsilon = 0.5% of entry fee.

My HU jam/fold Nash (chips, 169x169 equity by 20k-sample Monte Carlo per class pair with exact combo/card-removal weights, fictitious play; SP/pf/eq.c, SP/pf/pf.py): SB jam / BB call = 77.7/92.8% at 3BB, 71.4/62.1% at 5BB, 66.2/48.5% at 7BB, 58.3/37.5% at 10BB, 53.5/33.0% at 12BB, 45.7/28.2% at 15BB, 40.2/21.7% at 20BB, 36.1/17.4% at 25BB. SB value guaranteed by jam/fold (a lower bound on SB's full-game value, since BB can only call/fold vs a jam): +0.056 (5BB), +0.017 (7BB), -0.045 (10BB), -0.127 (15BB), -0.183 (20BB) BB/hand.

Exploitation magnitude, HU 10BB push/fold (SP/pf/exploit.py): SB best response vs a nit that calls top 15% gains +0.278 BB/hand over Nash (jams 100%); vs caller of top 70% +0.072; vs always-call +0.069 (Nash already +0.499). At 15BB vs nit +0.198.

One-step MMD update demo (SP/pf/mmdstep2.py; blueprint = Nash jam/fold smoothed eps=0.02, alpha=0.02, uniform magnet, exact q under the opponent model, 10BB): vs nit: eta=3 gain +0.042 BB/hand, worst-case value -0.067 (Nash -0.045); eta=10 gain +0.252 (91% of best response), worst-case -0.328; eta=inf +0.278 / -0.378. vs top-70% caller: eta=10 gain +0.062 (86% of BR) at worst-case -0.060.

HoldemResources/ICMIZER FGS = ICM plus simulation of following hands to capture blinds, position and blind rotation that ICM ignores (https://www.icmizer.com/en/blog/how-fgs-future-game-simulation-calculator-works/).

DeepStack (Science 2017; SP/lit/deepstack.txt:268-276, 368-372, 1176-1180): lookahead restricted to fold/call/2-3 bets/all-in, ~10^7 decision points re-solved in <5 s on a GTX 1080; turn net trained on 10M solved turn games using 6,144 CPU cores, >175 core-years; 486 mbb/g (AIVAT) vs pros; LBR cannot exploit it.

Libratus (Science 2018): 147 mbb/hand vs 4 pros over 120,000 hands (SP/lit/libratus.txt:380); nested safe subgame solving. Depth-limited solving / Modicum (Brown, Sandholm, Amos NeurIPS 2018; SP/lit/dls.txt:342-350): 700 core-hours blueprint, 4-core CPU and 16 GB at play, ~20 s per hand, beats Baby Tartanian8 (2M core-hours, 18 TB RAM) and Slumbot (250k core-hours, 2 TB RAM).

ReBeL (NeurIPS 2020; SP/lit/rebel.txt:492,535-545): data generation on up to 128 machines x 8 GPUs; vs Slumbot +45+-5 mbb/g, BabyTartanian8 +9+-4, Dong Kim +165+-69; poker code not released. Student of Games (Sci. Adv. 2023; SP/lit/sog.txt:532-544): beats Slumbot 7+-3 mbb/hand over 3.1M hands, LBR finds no exploit; TPU-scale training.

Pluribus (Science 2019; SP/lit/pluribus.txt:116-125,179-181,268-290): algorithms 'not guaranteed to converge to a Nash equilibrium outside of two-player zero-sum games'; blueprint 8 days on a 64-core server = 12,400 core-hours, <512 GB, ~$144; play on 2 CPUs <128 GB, 1-33 s per subgame search, ~20 s per hand; +48 mbb/g (SE 25) vs pros; 1-14 bet sizes per decision.

AlphaHoldem (AAAI 2022; SP/lit/ah.txt:38-41,105-112): end-to-end self-play RL (Trinal-Clip PPO, K-best historical pool), 3 days on one server with 8 GPUs + 64 CPU cores, 2.9 ms per decision on one GPU; beats Slumbot by 111.56 mbb/h and a DeepStack reimplementation by 16.91 mbb/h.

MMD (Sokota et al. ICLR 2023; SP/lit/mmd.txt:300-320,469-540,696): closed form pi_{t+1} ∝ [pi_t rho^{alpha eta} e^{eta q_t}]^{1/(1+alpha eta)}; benchmarks Kuhn, 2x2 Abrupt Dark Hex, 4-sided Liar's Dice, Leduc (54/471/8176/9300 non-terminal histories); exponential convergence to QRE; annealed-temperature and moving-magnet MMD 'competitive with (or better than) CFR' while CFR+ is best; F-FoReL takes ~200,000 iterations to reach 0.08 Leduc exploitability, MMD <1,000. Deep RL experiments were Dark Hex/Phantom TTT, not poker.

Update-equivalence (Sokota, Farina, Wu, Hu, Wang, Kolter, Brown ICLR 2024; SP/lit/ue.txt:280-300,1180-1200): MMDS update U(pi,q) ∝ [pi e^{eta q} rho^{eta alpha}]^{1/(1+alpha eta)}; tabular analogues converge empirically to AQRE and, with annealing, toward Nash on Kuhn and Leduc (Figs 1,6,7) but no formal 2p0s safety proof and no Hold'em experiments; Hanabi 24.62+-0.02 with two orders of magnitude less search; eta=50, alpha=0.01 in Dark Hex/PTTT.

Rudolph, ..., Farina, Vinitsky, Sokota 'Reevaluating Policy Gradient Methods for Imperfect-Information Games' (arXiv 2502.08938): over 7,000 runs / 345k CPU-hours NFSP, PSRO, ESCHER, R-NaD fail to outperform MMD/PPO/PPG (games up to 27M infostates, not poker).

Ataraxos text: public-information methods apply 'only when this amount is small, as in Texas hold'em (in which there are 1,326 possible hands)' (SP/paper.txt:28). Stratego search: reverse-KL to magnet 0.002, to policy net 0.02, 1,000 rollouts, depth 40 (SP/supp1.txt ~l.660-690, Table S12); implemented as logits' = (log pi + eta q + eta alpha log rho)/(1+eta alpha) in SP/stratego/pyengine/core/search.py:431-453 (equivalently eta = 1/0.02 = 50, alpha = 0.002).

Opponent modelling literature: Restricted Nash Response (Johanson, Zinkevich, Bowling NIPS 2007) pins opponent to the model with probability p; Data-Biased Response (Johanson & Bowling AISTATS 2009, SP/lit/dbr.txt) uses per-infoset confidence from observation counts and frequentist counts, fixing RNR overfitting; Safe opponent exploitation (Ganzfried & Sandholm, ACM TEAC 3(2) 2015) risks at most what was earned above equilibrium value; Bayes' Bluff (Southey et al. UAI 2005) gives a posterior over opponent strategies with Dirichlet or informed priors; Bayesian opponent exploitation (Ganzfried & Sun, arXiv 1603.03491) gives an exact Dirichlet-posterior best response; Online implicit agent modelling (Bard et al. AAMAS 2013) uses a portfolio plus bandit and would have won the 2011 ACPC HULHE exploitation event.

Showdown censoring: 'In poker-like games, folds hide private cards, so showdown data are missing not at random' so passive per-card estimators are inconsistent (Guo, arXiv 2608.09954, 2026; SP/lit/censor.txt:1-40). CodinGame reveals folded cards, so this bias is absent. Budgeted, certified restricted responses: Li & Huang arXiv 2607.28520 (Leduc: 6.2x the gain of a binary gate within budget).

3-player equilibria: Szafron, Gibson, Sturtevant AAMAS 2013 give a parameterised equilibrium family in 3-player Kuhn poker where one player can transfer utility to a second at the third's expense, with no 2-player analogue.

Leaderboard opponents are heterogeneous and exploitable (sibling analysis SP/stats3.py over replays): SmogyY (#14) and UnTypedScript (#23) open to 25-100BB and fold 0% vs <=3BB opens; kovi (#2) folds ~58-65% of unopened pots at every depth; BrandV jams 90% of first actions at <10BB and 66% at 10-20BB; open-size signatures differ per bot (e.g. MaxFerrer 2.5BB 90%, kozlov-ma 2.0BB 100%). This gives a behavioural fingerprint because names are not in the input.

Code budget: crossfish packs weights at 14 bits per counted character using CJK14 (/home/user/crossfish/documentation/minification.md:249-275); its 35,243-parameter NNUE takes 30,948 characters. So about 60-100k poker-net parameters at 8-12 bits fit next to about 30-40k characters of code.
design_implications:
Phase architecture:
- HU, effective stack ≲8-10BB: jam/fold Nash in chips as the prior. Precompute it offline; the 169-hand thresholds are tiny. Then take an exact KL-regularized best response to the posterior calling or jamming range, using the equity table (no rollouts needed).
- 3-4 handed, short stacks: ICM/TrueSkill-payout jam/fold as the prior, or the value head. Chip-EV ranges are too loose (60-74% equity needed to call off, versus 50%).
- Deeper stacks: MMD-PPO blueprint net plus one-step MMD search.

Exact belief (replaces the Ataraxos belief network). For opponent j with hidden combo y in C(52,2) = 1,326:
b_j(y | I) ∝ 1[y ∩ (x ∪ B) = ∅] · Π_{τ ∈ T_j(h)} σ_j(a_τ | y, B_τ, h_τ)
Here σ_j is the policy model used for j: π_θ (non-exploitative, as in Ataraxos) or the opponent model. The joint over opponents is exactly Π_j b_j(y_j) · 1[pairwise disjoint]. Sample it by rejection from the product of marginals; acceptance is high for 1-3 opponents. Update incrementally after each observed action. Add an ε-floor/mixture to σ so deterministic rule bots never produce zero likelihood.

Belief cost engineering:
- Factorize the net as logits(a|y,s) = g_a(s) + h_a(s)·e(y,B).
- e(y,B) is a small per-combo feature vector (hand strength vs uniform, draw potential, blockers), computed once per street for all 1,326 combos.
- Each observed action then costs 1,326 short dot products, a few tens of µs, instead of 1,326 full network evaluations.

Terminal utility U = Σ_p pay_p · P̂(place = p | stacks after hand, next button, next blind level).
- P̂ comes from a value head trained as a categorical over finishing places on self-play tournaments. This is a learned FGS/ICM that sees blind escalation and position, which ICM misses by up to $2.99 per $100 in Ganzfried-Sandholm's analysis.
- Fallback: Malmuth-Harville ICM with TrueSkill-implied payouts (1,.5,0) for 3p and (1,.645,.355,0) for 4p. HU: U ≈ stack/4800.
- Busted players take places by bust order, with the tie rule of Board.java:555-578.

Search step (the Ataraxos/UE closed form):
π_s(a|I) ∝ exp{ [log π_θ(a|I) + η·q̂(a) + ηα·log ρ(a|I)] / (1 + ηα) }
The Stratego form ∝ [e^q̂ ρ^0.002 π_θ^0.02]^{1/(0.002+0.02)} is η = 50, α = 0.002, with q in win-probability units. Sample the move from π_s.
- Scale: η·Δq should be O(1) logits. In equity units per-decision Δq is ~0.001-0.05, so η ~ 20-500. In HU chip-EV/BB units η ~ 0.3-10.
- Noise control: pick η so that η·σ_Δ/√K ≲ 0.3, or shrink q̂(a) ← q̂(a)·K/(K + σ̂_a²/τ²).

Safety bound, and η as a risk budget. With α = 0: KL(π_s‖π_θ) ≤ η·(max_a q̂ − ⟨π_θ, q̂⟩) ≤ η·R̂, where R̂ = range of q̂. By Pinsker, for any true action-value vector q* (e.g. against a best-responding opponent) with range R*: ⟨π_s − π_θ, q*⟩ ≥ −(R*/2)·√(2η·R̂).
This is a local, per-decision bound. Schedule η_t so that the bound stays ≤ max(ε, κ·G_t), where G_t is the estimated cumulative gain over the blueprint this game (Ganzfried-Sandholm 'risk only what you've won').
In the 10BB demo, η = 3 keeps worst-case loss within 0.022 BB/hand of Nash; η = 10 captures 91% of the best-response gain vs a nit but is highly exploitable.

Plugging in the opponent model while keeping KL-to-prior safety:
- Use σ_j = λ_j·π̂_j + (1 − λ_j)·π_θ, with DBR-style confidence λ_j = n_j/(n_j + n_0) per situation bucket.
- Use the same σ_j in both the belief likelihood and the rollouts.
- Keep π_θ (not π̂) as the KL anchor, and ρ as the magnet.
- The result is a KL-regularized best response to the model: η → 0 recovers the blueprint, η → ∞ gives the full best response to the model.

Online opponent model from complete data. Every hand reveals every hole card, so each opponent decision is a labelled triple (y, s, a) and the likelihood Π log σ(a|y,s) is exact (no marginalization, no censoring bias).
- With ~55-63 decisions per opponent per game (only 14-23 postflop), fit only a few parameters.
- Option 1: logits = prior logits + Φ(s,y)ᵀw_j, with 20-60 features (street × facing-bet × hand-strength tercile × action type), w_j ~ N(0, Σ0), a couple of Newton/MAP steps per hand.
- Option 2: a Bayesian type posterior over a library of behaviour-cloned leaderboard bots, P(k|D) ∝ P(k)·Π σ_k(a|y,s). Train the library offline from replays, which contain all cards. Use bet-size signatures to fingerprint, since names are not in the input.
- In the current hand, infer type and combo jointly: b(y,k|h) ∝ P(k|D)·prior(y)·Π σ_k(a_τ|y,s_τ).

Training the blueprint (the directly transferable Ataraxos component):
- Environment: C++ clone of the referee (min-raise rules, action replacement, blind schedule, elimination tie rule).
- Episodes: whole tournaments with n ∈ {2,3,4}; reward = TrueSkill payout at the end.
- Loss: PPO-clip + 0.1·KL(π‖π_old) + α_t·KL(π‖ρ) + value cross-entropy over places; anneal α_t and the learning rate by power laws.
- Opponent pool: past checkpoints (AlphaHoldem K-best) plus scripted exploitable bots and leaderboard clones, so the net learns implicit modelling from public per-opponent statistics fed as inputs.
- Guarantees: MMD's QRE→Nash guarantee holds only in the HU (constant-sum) phase; 3-4p is heuristic, as it is for Pluribus/CFR.

Poker-specific variance reduction:
- Privileged critic that sees all hole cards as the PPO baseline (still unbiased, since the baseline depends on state, not action).
- All-in EV substitution in returns: replace dealt runouts with equity.
- AIVAT-style correction for evaluation.
- Apply Ataraxos advantage filtering (top-25% |A|, ≥0.01) only after these steps. On raw returns, card luck dominates and filtering would select noise.

Budget at 50 ms in C++:
- Small-MLP evaluation ~10 µs, table-based 7-card evaluator ~50 ns.
- That gives ~500-1,000 rollouts of 4-6 decisions, i.e. ~100-200 per action across 5-7 actions.
- Use common random numbers, exact all-in/river equity, and a street-boundary value-net cutoff to stretch the budget.
- Use the 1,000 ms first turn to unpack CJK14 weights and build equity/rank tables.
- Keep the net ≤~60-100k parameters (14 bits/char, as in crossfish), not the Ataraxos dou dizhu/Hanabi sizes (1.9M-5.9M).

Multi-way specifics:
- Rollouts include all live players with their own σ_j; the joint belief uses rejection on card removal.
- Terminal values are ICM/place-based, so 'let the others bust each other' survival play emerges. Two-big-stack confrontations need ~74% equity.
- There is no exploitability guarantee (Szafron kingmaker effect, Pluribus caveat). Treat the KL to π_θ as a regularizer toward self-play-consistent play, not as a proof of safety.

Opponent bet sizes: feed an opponent's exact continuous bet/pot ratio and stack-to-pot ratio into the net features. This avoids the action translation that tabular-abstraction bots need (Libratus/Pluribus rely on search for off-tree sizes). Only our own outputs are discretized.
open_questions: Does unrestricted HU play (limp/min-raise) beat jam/fold at 10-20BB, and by how much in BB/hand? My jam/fold SB value turns negative above ~8BB, but only a full short-stack HU solve (e.g. MCCFR at 10-25BB with a coarse abstraction) can quantify the gap.

Are TrueSkill payouts at equal ratings the right utility? Against opponents of very different ratings, the mu deltas per place change. It may be better to learn the utility per matchup or simply to use the place-distribution value head.

How many rollouts per action fit in 50 ms on CodinGame hardware, and is K ≈ 100-200 enough given the high variance of hand outcomes? This needs measurement. Exact river/all-in equity and a street-boundary value cutoff may be necessary.

Can leaderboard bots be fingerprinted reliably within the first ~10-20 hands (bet-size signatures, open sizes), given that names are not in the input? Is a behaviour-cloned library of the top ~50 bots worth its characters in the 100k budget, compared with a generic few-parameter adaptive model?

Is MMD-PPO self-play stable and useful in 3-4 player tournaments? Would a population or opponent-pool approach (K-best checkpoints plus scripted exploitable bots) produce a blueprint that is too exploitative or not exploitative enough against the real field?
Should advantage filtering be used at all, given poker's chance variance, or only once a privileged critic and all-in EV substitution are in place?

The sibling scratch files include seed-recovery scripts (SP/poker_research/recover_seed.py, javacheck/RngDump.java). I did not investigate or rely on predicting the deck, and it would likely violate the spirit of the rules.

research.summary:
Short answer: a CodinGame Poker bot in C++ can carry about 80-140k int8 network parameters in the source file. Inside 40 ms it can run a few thousand evaluations of a ~100k-parameter MLP, an exact Bayesian range update over all 1,326 hands per opponent action, and a one-step MMD search with about 2-5k short rollouts. That is roughly the rollout count Ataraxos used (dou dizhu 200, Stratego 1,000, Hanabi 10,000), with a network 20-60 times smaller. Offline training of a network this small costs about 10^9 samples a day on CPU, far below the paper's GPU budgets.

Platform limits, checked:
- Source cap is 100k characters, counted as UTF-16 units.
- Memory is 768 MB.
- C++ is g++ 11.2. The help page (archived Feb 2026) says "mode C++20"; the user's CI-verified line is `-std=gnu++17 -Werror=return-type -g -pthread` with no -O. The user's rules therefore still apply: `#pragma GCC optimize("O3")` before the includes, `always_inline` on hot helpers, no std containers in hot code, AVX2 target pragma after the includes.
- The referee gives 1000 ms for the first turn and 50 ms after that; a timeout eliminates the player. The 600 "rounds" count player actions.
- In 120 real top-bot replays the round cap never bound (max 339). A bot makes at most about 140 decisions per game (median 63-77). Median game length is 42-46 hands (max 69), and 61% of decisions are preflop.

Payload: CJK14 gives 14 bits per character, against 6 for base64. With about 20k characters of minified code and 3k safety margin there are about 77k payload characters, about 1.08 Mbit. After the tables below (8.3k chars), that leaves room for:

| Precision | Parameters |
| --- | --- |
| user's Rice/GPTQ, 12.3 bits | ~78k |
| int8 | ~120k |
| ~6-bit Rice | ~160k |
| int4 | ~240k |

Base64 would cut every figure by a factor of 2.3.

Tables:
- The 169x169 HU preflop equity matrix (14,196 unique entries) costs 8.1k characters at 8 bits. Computing it at start-up is not viable: 20k trials per pair took 4.0 s on 4 threads.
- HU Nash push/fold charts stored as per-hand stack thresholds cost about 194 characters. The equilibrium can also be solved at runtime from the 169x169 table. My fictitious-play solver reproduces the published Nash values: at 10 BB the small blind pushes 58.0% and the big blind calls 37.3%. 2,000 iterations take 86 ms as written (not yet vectorized); 300-500 iterations fit in a turn.
- 3-handed ICM charts on a 10-level stack grid would be about 4k characters. 4-handed would be about 86k, which does not fit, so 3-4 handed spots need runtime solving or the policy net.
- Flop hand-strength bucket tables (1.29M canonical hand/flop pairs) do not fit. Compute them at runtime instead (numbers below).

Evaluator: I wrote pe7c.hpp and benchmarked it under CodinGame's command line.
- Design: OMPEval's 13 additive rank keys, a perfect hash (rows of 256, offsets computed at start-up) and a flush-mask table. Everything is computed at start-up, so there is no payload.
- Size: 2,658 characters after the user's minifier.
- Start-up: 62-85 ms, about 1.1 MB of tables.
- Speed: 236-284 M random 7-card evaluations/s including building the hand, and 1.0-1.25 G/s when enumerating.
- Correctness: all 9 hand-category counts over the full 133,784,560-hand enumeration match, with 4,824 distinct classes. Ordering never disagreed with OMPEval or HenryRLee's evaluator on 524,288 random pairs.
- Comparison on this machine: OMPEval 356 M/s, but it needs a 102 KB offset table. HenryRLee's evaluator is 49 M/s with about 340 KB of tables. Rebuilding with 4096-wide rows at start-up took 1.1-1.6 s, too slow for the first turn. A 67 MB direct-lookup variant runs at 123 M/s random. Two-plus-two (130 MB) and SKPokerEval (315 KB of tables) do not fit.

Runtime primitives, measured single-thread with CodinGame's compile line:
- Monte Carlo HU equity: 31-32M trials/s, about 1.1M trials in 35 ms.
- Exact equity of one hand vs a random hand: 0.07-0.12 ms on the turn, 2.4-3.6 ms on the flop.
- Exact equity of all 1,326 hands vs a weighted range (card-removal aware): 16 µs river, 0.88 ms turn, 20.6 ms flop.
- fp32 AVX2 MLP, per evaluation (single → batched):

| Parameters | µs per evaluation |
| --- | --- |
| 8.8k | 0.43-0.54 |
| 34k | 1.3-1.9 |
| 101k | 3.9-5.4 |
| 265k | 10-14 |

What fits in 40 ms:
- **Bayesian range update:** about 1,225 hands x (#opponent actions) network evaluations. With the private-card first-layer trick from the user's NNUE, that is about 3 ms per opponent action for a 100k net and about 1.2 ms for a 34k net. This is fine heads-up; 4-handed with up to 6 actions per turn it is tight for the 100k net.
- **One-step MMD search:** each rollout costs about (remaining decisions ≈ 3) x network cost + leaf. Using exact runout equity at the leaf also cuts variance. That gives about 2,400 rollouts with a 100k net or about 5,000 with a 34k net, so about 400-1,000 per action for 5-6 abstract actions.

Offline training: I count about 8P FLOP per sample: generation plus 4 PPO epochs on the 25% advantage-filtered samples. For P = 100k that is 0.8 PFLOP per 10^9 samples.
- On this 4-vCPU box, numpy training runs at 27k samples/s (100k MLP) and 91k/s (34k MLP). With C++ self-play at about 4 µs per decision per core, that is about 11 hours per 10^9 samples.
- On one GPU the math takes minutes, so a vectorized game environment becomes the bottleneck; 10^10 samples a day is plausible.
- Reference points: AlphaHoldem used 6.5B samples in 3 days on 8 GPUs and 64 cores (4,000 CPU-hours, 580 GPU-hours, 98 MB model). Ataraxos used 1 L40 for 2 days (Hanabi, 5.9M parameters), 4 H100 for 2 days (dou dizhu, 1.9M) and 16 H100 for a week (Stratego, under $8k).

All timings come from this sandbox (Xeon @ 2.1 GHz, g++ 13.3, not 11.2). CodinGame's hardware is unknown, so budgets should be scaled by a benchmark run during the first turn.

design_implications: Use C++ (the user's toolchain). Budget the source as about 15-25k minified code chars + 3k margin + about 72-82k CJK14 payload chars (1.0-1.15 Mbit).

Recommended network: one shared-trunk MLP of about 100k params, e.g. ~128 engineered inputs -> 256 -> 256 -> heads of ~8 abstract actions (fold, check/call, 0.33/0.5/0.75/1/1.5 pot, all-in) + value. At int8 that is about 57.7k CJK14 chars; at the user's 12-14-bit GPTQ/Rice scheme it is about 88k and does not fit alongside everything else. So use int8 or ~6-bit Rice. If 4-handed range updates are too slow, drop to about 34k params (1.3 us/eval) or split policy (~64k) and value (~34k).

Inputs should include evaluator-computed features that a tiny net cannot learn cheaply: exact equity vs the current Bayesian range (river 16 us, turn 0.9 ms, flop ~3 ms for our hand or ~21 ms for all hands), pot odds, stacks/BB per seat, position, street, blind level, players alive, and ICM/finish-position equity.

Replace Ataraxos's belief transformer with an exact Bayesian filter over 1,326 hands per opponent, using the self-play policy's likelihoods: about 1,225 net evals per observed opponent action (~3 ms at 100k with the NNUE-style private-card first-layer cache). With 3 opponents, keep independent per-opponent ranges and resolve card conflicts by rejection sampling.

Test-time search: one closed-form MMD step, logits' = (log pi + eta*q_hat + eta*alpha*log rho)/(1+eta*alpha), over ~5-6 actions. Estimate q_hat with batched (B=16) lockstep rollouts of the policy for all players to the end of the hand, and exact runout equity at all-in/showdown leaves to cut variance. This gives about 2.4k (100k net) to 5k (34k net) rollouts in 35 ms. Check the clock every ~16 rollouts; keep a hard cap of about 35-40 ms because a timeout eliminates.

Embed (a) the 169x169 HU preflop equity matrix at 8 bits (8.1k chars) and (b) HU Nash push/fold thresholds (~194 chars) to use as the magnet/prior or a fallback for shallow HU stacks. Solve other push/fold variants at runtime with a few hundred fictitious-play iterations (vectorize to reach ~10-20 ms). Do not embed 4-handed ICM charts (~86k chars); leave 3-4-handed short-stack play to the policy net trained with a finish-position reward.

Ship pe7c.hpp (2.7k chars, 62-85 ms start-up, about 240 M/s random): no payload is needed. Do not use two-plus-two (130 MB), SKPokerEval/PHEvaluator tables (300+ KB of literals), or OMPEval's precomputed 102 KB offsets; the direct 67 MB table is a simpler fallback at half the random-access speed.

First turn (1000 ms): evaluator start-up (<=85 ms), payload decode/dequantize (<1 ms for 100k params), table decode, plus a 20-50 ms benchmark of evals/s and MLP us/eval printed to stderr, to scale rollout and range-update budgets to CG's real CPU.

Training plan: C++ self-play environment reusing the bot's evaluator and inference code; MMD-in-PPO (0.1*KL to old policy + annealed alpha*KL to magnet) with advantage filtering; about 8*P FLOP per sample, so 0.8 PFLOP per 1e9 samples at P=100k. CPU-only is about 11 h per 1e9 samples on 4 vCPUs (~1e9 samples/day on an 8-16-core desktop). One rented GPU with a vectorized environment reaches about 1e10/day. Plan for 1e9-1e10 decisions (AlphaHoldem used 6.5e9 with a ~100x larger net).

Train per-hand episodes with a finish-position (ICM-like) utility for 3-4 players and chip EV for HU (HU win probability is linear in chips), covering 2, 3 and 4 player tables and the doubling blind schedule. The observed regime mix (HU 42% of decisions <=25BB; 4-handed 79% >50BB) means both deep and shallow play matter.

All cards (including folded hands) are revealed at hand end, which is free labelled data for opponent modelling. Ataraxos's search is non-exploitative by design, but the magnet rho or the rollout policies could be shifted toward an online-fitted opponent model as a later extension.

Exact CG C++ mode: the help page says g++ 11.2 'mode C++20', the user's CI-verified line says -std=gnu++17. Printing __cplusplus to stderr on CG settles it; my benchmarks used g++ 13.3 with the gnu++17 line, not 11.2 (the user's gcc:11.2 docker gate can re-time them).

How much of the 50 ms CG spends on I/O and process scheduling (safe usable budget is probably 35-42 ms), and how often latency spikes occur. A timeout eliminates the player, so the margin should be set from measured CG timings.
Samples needed for MMD-PPO to converge on 2-4 player escalating-blind sit-and-gos with a ~100k-param MLP (my 1e9-1e10 estimate extrapolates from AlphaHoldem and the Ataraxos runs, not from a pilot).
Whether 3-4-handed short-stack play needs dedicated push/fold solving at runtime (multiway equities via MC: about 20M 3-way trials/s) or whether the policy net plus MMD search handles it well enough.
Whether 8-bit quantization is enough for policy logits and range updates, or whether 6-bit Rice with GPTQ (the user's pipeline) is needed to fit ~150k params.

designs.name: Ataraxos-Poker: MMD-PPO tournament blueprint + exact-range update-equivalence search (CodinGame NLHE SNG, 2-4 players)
designs.thesis:
Yes, the recipe transfers. Poker only needs about half of it, and two parts must be recalibrated or they quietly break.

**Kept close to the paper:**
- The trained artifact is one small last-iterate policy/value net, trained by dynamically damped self-play. The loss is MMD inside PPO: PPO-clip + 0.1*KL(pi||pi_old) + alpha_t*KL(pi||uniform magnet) + categorical value cross-entropy, with power-law schedules on alpha and the learning rate, advantage filtering, and EMA weights (stratego/pyengine/core/rl.py:549-579, 756; buffer.py:240).
- It plays through one closed-form update-equivalence step at test time: logits' = (log pi_theta + eta*q_hat + eta*alpha*log rho)/(1 + eta*alpha) (search.py:431-453), with q_hat from policy rollouts over hidden states drawn from a belief.

**Dropped, because Stratego needed them and poker does not:**
- The belief transformer becomes an exact Bayes filter over <=1,326 combos per opponent, using the policy net's own likelihoods (the paper itself notes Hold'em's 1,326 hands, paper.txt:28).
- Depth-40 rollouts plus a value net become rollouts to the end of the current hand (<=~12 decisions). All-in and showdown leaves use exact enumeration of the remaining board cards, and hand-end stacks are scored by a tiny learned tournament-value net W (a learned FGS/ICM).
- The setup network goes (poker has no setup phase), and the 1.9-5.9M-parameter nets shrink to ~80k int8 parameters so they fit in 100k characters via CJK14.

**Changed, with honest caveats:**
1. **Reward.** It is the rank payout that TrueSkill implies ((1,0), (1,.5,0), (1,.645,.355,0)), not +/-1. So 3-4 player play is constant-sum but not two-player zero-sum, and MMD's convergence guarantee to QRE/Nash holds only once the table is heads-up.
2. **Scale.** 1 BB is worth 0.002-0.08 payout units depending on blind level and player count; I computed this with ICM in pf/icm2.py (HU 2400/2400: 0.0021 at 5/10 and 0.033 at 80/160; 4p short stack at 80/160: 0.080). With Ataraxos's absolute temperatures (alpha 0.1 down to 0.001) and filter threshold (|A| >= 0.01), early-level play would be close to uniform and almost all early decisions would be filtered out. So every advantage and every q is re-expressed in BB-equivalents: divide by the local chip-to-payout slope s = dW_me/dchips * BB.
3. **Chance variance.** Poker's chance variance makes raw advantage filtering select card luck. It only becomes useful after a privileged (all-cards) critic, substituting exact equity once players are all-in, and bootstrapping at hand boundaries.
4. **Bet sizes.** Our own sizes are discretised. Opponents' continuous sizes go into the net as features, and pseudo-harmonic interpolation is used only inside the belief likelihood.
5. **Exploitation.** The faithful bot is non-exploitative by design, but the field is full of exploitable heuristic bots (#1 finishes ahead of a given top-league opponent only 61%). So the last milestone plugs an online opponent model into the same belief and rollout machinery, with the KL-to-pi_theta term (eta) serving as the safety dial.

components.name: Referee-exact C++ engine (training env + in-bot rollout engine)
components.description:
A C++ port of the Python referee port poker_sim.py (scratchpad/poker_research/), used both as the vectorised self-play environment and, stripped down, as the rollout engine inside the bot.

It must reproduce these rules exactly:
- Every non-BB player posts the SB (Board.java:204-218), so the preflop pot is 1.5/2/2.5 BB.
- A short-blind poster is forced all-in.
- The preflop call is at least one BB.
- The minimum raise is measured from the last full raise; after a short all-in only the last full raiser is locked (ActionUtils.java:443-464).
- The raise cap is 10 raises per street.
- Side pots with odd chips.
- NONE rounds.
- The 600-decision cap with refund.
- Bust-order scoring, with same-hand busts ordered by chips put in.

Acceptance: reproduce 120/120 replays via validate_replays.py, plus a 1e6-hand differential fuzz against poker_sim.py with random actions and sizes. The in-bot copy covers only the single-hand betting logic plus pot resolution.
components.cost_estimate: ~5k minified chars in the bot. Offline ~0.5-1 us per env step per core without net inference. 3-5 days of work.

components.name: 7-card evaluator pe7c.hpp
components.cost_estimate: 2,658 chars. 62-85 ms at first-turn start-up, ~1.1 MB of tables. 236-284M random evaluations/s.

components.name: Feature extractor phi(s, y)
components.cost_estimate: ~3k chars. ~1 us per decision in training (MC-64 EHS). <=1 ms per new street for all 1,326 combos in the bot.

components.name: Policy net pi_theta (with a small place head)
components.cost_estimate: int8 with a bf16 per-row scale: ~80.3 KB, about 46k CJK14 chars. Alternatively ~6-bit Rice/GPTQ from the crossfish pipeline for ~120-130k params in the same space. ~3-4 us per evaluation single, ~2.5 us batched (scaled from the measured 101k net at 3.9-5.4 us). ~2-2.5 us per combo with the split first layer.

components.name: Tournament value net W (learned FGS/ICM)
components.description:
W(public hand-start state) gives the expected TrueSkill payout for each seat.

Inputs: stacks/BB for 4 seats, button/SB/BB seats, N alive, log2 BB, hands until the next doubling, round/600.

Architecture: 16 -> 64 -> 64 -> 4, with a softmax over the place distribution per seat, then combined with the payouts (1,.645,.355,0) or (1,.5,0) or (1,0).

Training is by TD on hand-start states from self-play tournaments. It is initialised by regressing onto Malmuth-Harville ICM (pf/icm2.py) and refit every ~50 training steps, because W depends on the policy.

Uses:
- every rollout leaf at hand end: E_runouts[W(stacks')];
- the chip-to-payout slope s used for BB-normalisation;
- the hand-boundary bootstrap in training.

Fallback: exact ICM (0.5k chars). Also used in training as part of the privileged critic.
components.cost_estimate: ~5k params, ~3k chars at int8. ~0.2 us per evaluation.

components.name: Privileged critic V_priv (training only)
components.description:
A larger MLP (~0.3-1M params) that sees every seat's hole cards, the board, the betting state and the tournament state. It outputs an N x N place distribution (categorical, trained with cross-entropy, like Ataraxos's use_cat_vf).

It is the PPO/GAE baseline. That stays unbiased because the actor's action distribution depends only on its infostate, which is a subset of the full state.

At hand boundaries it must agree with W: W is its restriction to states with no cards dealt. It is never embedded, so its size is free.
components.cost_estimate: Negligible next to generating samples on a GPU. On CPU it roughly doubles training FLOPs.

components.name: MMD-in-PPO trainer (Ataraxos RL, poker-calibrated)
components.description:
Episodes are whole sit-and-go tournaments with N sampled as 25/34/41% for 2/3/4 players (the arena mix) and a random first BB. All seats play the same current policy (pure self-play, last iterate, EMA weights shipped).

Advantages:
- GAE with lambda = 0.9 inside a hand.
- At the hand boundary, bootstrap with W (cross-hand lambda = 0), because card luck in later hands only adds variance.
- Once everyone is all-in, replace the dealt runout with the exact expectation over runouts.
- Divide by the local slope s(state) so advantages are in BB-equivalents. This amounts to an infostate-specific QRE temperature, which is what keeps the magnet term meaningful at every blind level.

Loss (as rl.py:549-579): PPO-clip(0.2) + 0.1*KL(pi||pi_old) + alpha_t*KL(pi||uniform over legal) + value cross-entropy.

Schedules (Ataraxos power_schedule shape):
- alpha_t = clip(0.5*(t+1)^-0.35, 0.02, 0.5) in BB units. Stratego's absolute 0.05*(t+1)^-0.3 clipped to [0.001, 0.1] is not usable directly, because 1 BB = 0.002-0.08 payout.
- Learning rate clip(0.03*(t+1)^-0.5, 3e-5, 1e-3) for Adam on the small MLP.

Advantage filter (buffer.py:240: top 25% of |A| and |A| >= threshold): the threshold is rescaled to 0.05 BB. It is enabled only after the critic is working, and ablated at filter rates 0, 0.5 and 0.75.

Training-time size jitter: with probability 0.5, multiply our raise fraction by exp(U(-0.25, 0.25)), so the net learns to face continuous opponent sizes.
components.cost_estimate:
~8P FLOP per sample, about 0.64 MFLOP at P = 80k, so ~0.6 PFLOP per 1e9 decisions.
- CPU only: ~1e9 decisions/day on a 16-core desktop.
- 1 GPU plus a 16-32-core C++ environment: ~5e9-1e10 per day.
- Plan for 3-10e9 decisions (AlphaHoldem used 6.5e9 with a ~100x larger net): about $50-150 of rented GPU/CPU time.

components.name: Exact Bayesian range tracker (replaces the belief transformer)
components.description:
For each opponent j, keep b_j[1326]. The update is
b_j(y) proportional to 1[y disjoint from my cards and the board] * product over j's actions this hand of L(a_tau | y, s_tau).

The likelihood is
L = (1 - eps) * pi_theta(a~ | phi(s_tau, y)) + eps/|A|, with eps = 0.03, which guards against zero likelihood from deterministic rule bots.

For an off-tree opponent size f between abstract sizes f_A and f_B, use the pseudo-harmonic weight
w = ((f_B - f)(1 + f_A)) / ((f_B - f_A)(1 + f)), and set L = w*pi(A|y) + (1 - w)*pi(B|y).

Cost control:
- Preflop, update over 169 classes and then expand to combos.
- Postflop, skip combos with b < 1e-4 * max.
- Recompute the cached private features when a new street card arrives.

Joint sampling over opponents: rejection from the product of marginals, subject to disjoint cards (acceptance > 85% with <=3 opponents).
components.cost_estimate: ~1.5k chars. 1,326 floats per opponent. ~0.4 ms per preflop action, ~0.5-3 ms per postflop action. Hard cap of 12 ms per turn, falling back to 64 EHS buckets.

components.name: Update-equivalence one-step search
components.description:
For each legal abstract action a, and for k = 1..K with common random numbers across actions (the same sampled hidden hands and the same deck permutation):
- play a;
- then all players, including us, sample actions from pi_theta, in lockstep batches of 16 rollouts, until the hand ends or a depth cap of 12 is reached;
- at the leaf, take the exact expectation over remaining boards of W_me(stacks'), or use the place head at the cap.

Then:
- q_hat(a) = mean_k(q_k(a)) / s, i.e. in BB-equivalents.
- Shrink q_hat toward its mean with tau = 2 BB.
- pi_s = softmax[(log pi_theta + eta*q + eta*alpha*log rho)/(1 + eta*alpha)], with rho uniform over legal actions, eta ~ 1.5 per BB (tuned between 0.5 and 3) and alpha = 0.05, so eta*alpha ~ 0.075 (Stratego: 0.1).
- Sample the move from pi_s.

The KL-to-policy term is kept because it matters in poker for the same reason as in Stratego: rollouts assume everyone plays pi_theta. The one-step bound KL(pi_s||pi_theta) <= eta*range(q) limits the damage from noisy or misspecified q.
components.cost_estimate: ~3k chars. ~12-15 us per rollout, so ~2,000 rollouts in 25 ms, i.e. K ~ 250-400 per action for 5-7 legal actions. Paper reference points: dou dizhu 200 rollouts, Stratego 1,000.

components.name: Push/fold and ICM reference solutions
components.description:
- HU Nash jam/fold from the 169x169 equity table by fictitious play (pf/pf.py). Reference values at 10 BB: SB jams 58%, BB calls 37%.
- 3-player ICM jam/fold by value iteration plus fictitious play, as in Ganzfried and Sandholm (AAMAS 2008).

They are not used as the magnet (the faithful design keeps a uniform magnet). Their uses are:
1. evaluation oracles: the learned blueprint's short-stack regret against them;
2. an emergency fallback when a timer check fails before search completes.
The optional 169x169 table (8.1k chars) makes heads-up preflop all-in leaves exact.
components.cost_estimate: HU thresholds: 194 chars. 169x169 table optional at 8.1k chars; otherwise 256-sample Monte Carlo at the leaf (~4 us).

components.name: Packing and minification
components.cost_estimate: ~2 days, reusing crossfish tooling.

components.name: Local arena and baseline zoo
components.cost_estimate: ~3-4 days of work. A search bot costs ~2.4 s of CPU per game (~60 decisions x 40 ms), so 10k games take ~25 min on 16 cores.

designs.per_turn_algorithm:
The clock starts when the first stdin line of the turn has been read. Hard deadline: 40 ms of wall time (the limit is 50 ms, and a timeout eliminates the bot). Budgets are rescaled by a benchmark run on the first turn.

**First turn only (1000 ms available):**
- Build the pe7c tables: ~85 ms.
- CJK14-decode and dequantise the weights: <5 ms.
- Build the 169-class tables.
- Run a 20 ms benchmark of MLP us/eval and evaluator evals/s, and print __cplusplus and the timings to stderr.
- Then run the normal pipeline with a search budget of ~600 ms.

**Every turn:**

**1. Parse (<0.2 ms).**
- Read the round, handNb, stacks and chipInPot, board, our cards, the action lines since our last turn and the showdown lines.
- Rebuild seats, dealer/SB/BB (firstBigBlindId plus rotation of the BB to the next seat with chips), per-street bets, lastTotalRoundBet, the minimum raise (checked against the BET_x hint) and the raise count.
- On a new hand, reset the ranges to uniform over combos that do not conflict with known cards.
- (M5 only) Log the revealed hole cards from the showdown lines for the opponent model.

**2. New street (<=1 ms).**
- Zero out combos that conflict with the board.
- Recompute the cached private features x(y) for all live combos: made-hand rank percentile, MC-32 EHS/EHS^2, draw flags.

**3. Range updates (<=12 ms cap; typically 1-4 ms).**
For each opponent action in the history, in order:
- Rebuild that seat's public features p once and compute the first-layer partial sum A*p.
- For each live combo, compute pi_theta(.|y), in 169 classes preflop.
- Take the likelihood of the observed action. An off-tree size uses pseudo-harmonic interpolation between the adjacent abstract sizes, with an eps = 0.03 floor.
- Multiply into the range and renormalise.
If the cap is reached, finish the remaining actions with 64 EHS buckets.

**4. Blueprint (<0.1 ms).**
- Compute pi_theta(.|our infostate) over the 8 abstract actions, with the legal mask and deduplication (sizes that collapse to MIN or ALL-IN).
- If there is one legal action, or a trivial spot (checking is free and the only alternative is folding), answer immediately.

**5. Scale (<0.01 ms).**
- s = local chip-to-payout slope from W by finite difference, times BB. So q is measured in BB-equivalents: 1 BB = 0.002-0.08 payout.

**6. Rollouts (until 37 ms).**
Loop over k:
- Sample the opponents' hidden hands jointly from the ranges (rejection on disjointness) and one deck permutation (common random numbers).
- For every legal action a: apply a, then simulate every live player with pi_theta (softmax sampling), batched 16 rollouts in lockstep for SIMD, until the hand ends or depth 12.
- Leaves:
  - a fold gives stacks' directly;
  - an all-in or showdown uses the exact expectation over remaining boards (river 1, turn ~44, flop 990 runouts; heads-up preflop uses the 169x169 table or MC-256; multiway preflop uses MC-256). Accumulate E[W_me(stacks')] per distinct outcome, because W is nonlinear in stacks;
  - at the depth cap, use the place head.
- Check the clock every 16 rollouts.
- Expect ~2,000 rollouts, i.e. K ~ 250-400 per action.

**7. q-hat.**
- q_hat(a) = mean_k(q_k(a))/s.
- James-Stein-style shrink toward the pi_theta-weighted mean: q~ = qbar + (q_hat - qbar) * K/(K + sigma_a^2/tau^2), with tau = 2 BB.

**8. MMD step (Ataraxos closed form).**
- logits'(a) = (log pi_theta(a) + eta*q~(a) + eta*alpha*log rho(a))/(1 + eta*alpha)
- eta = 1.5 per BB (a tuned constant; later scaled by rollout confidence so that eta*SE <= 0.3), alpha = 0.05, rho uniform over legal actions.
- Sample a ~ softmax(logits').

**9. Emit (<0.05 ms).**
- FOLD -> "FOLD".
- CHECK/CALL -> "CALL" (always safe: it becomes CHECK or ALL-IN as needed; never print CHECK when facing a bet).
- A raise to R -> "BET x" with x = max(BET_min, R - myStreetBet). If x >= stack, print "ALL-IN".
- Append ";" plus a short debug message (top q values).
- If the clock passes 40 ms at any point, emit the blueprint argmax. A timer fault before step 4 falls back to the push/fold chart or "CALL".
designs.training_pipeline:
